pos: n. pl. (lovers of wisdom; the professional thinkers Paul met at Athens; rendering Greek philosophos)
etymology: Greek philos, loving, and sophia, wisdom — a word Pythagoras is said to have coined out of modesty, since only God is wise and a man may at most love wisdom.
biblical_def: The only appearance of the word: “Then certain philosophers of the Epicureans, and of the Stoicks, encountered him. And some said, What will this babbler say?” (Act 17:18). Paul's assessment of the guild is not dismissive but exact: “Where is the wise? where is the scribe? where is the disputer of this world? hath not God made foolish the wisdom of this world?” (1Co 1:20); “the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God” (1Co 3:19). Yet on Mars' hill he quoted their own poets approvingly — “as certain also of your own poets have said, For we are also his offspring” (Act 17:28) — and the warning is against being carried off, not against thinking: “Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit” (Col 2:8).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines philosopher as a person versed in philosophy, or in the principles of nature and morality; one who devotes himself to the study of the phenomena of nature and their causes.
webster_full: PHILOSOPHER, n. A person versed in philosophy, or in the principles of nature and morality.
2. One who devotes himself to the study of the phenomena of nature, and their causes and effects.
3. In a general sense, one who is profoundly versed in any science.
scriptures: Then certain philosophers of the Epicureans, and of the Stoicks, encountered him. And some said, What will this babbler say? other some, He seemeth to be a setter forth of strange gods: because he preached unto them Jesus, and the resurrection.
Where is the wise? where is the scribe? where is the disputer of this world? hath not God made foolish the wisdom of this world?
For the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God. For it is written, He taketh the wise in their own craftiness.
For in him we live, and move, and have our being; as certain also of your own poets have said, For we are also his offspring.
Col 2:8
Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men, after the rudiments of the world, and not after Christ.
corruption_summary: Philosophy is either despised outright or allowed to set the questions, and Paul at Athens did neither.
corruption_paragraphs: Acts 17 is the model and it refuses both easy positions. Paul does not flee the philosophers, and he does not flatter them. He walks their city, reads their altars, quotes two of their poets from memory, and builds an address that starts where they are and ends where they cannot follow — at a Man whom God hath raised from the dead, at which point some mocked, some deferred, and some clave unto him and believed. That is the whole method: engagement without surrender, and a conclusion that the audience has not been softened up to accept.

Colossians 2:8 gives the danger with a precise verb. Beware lest any man spoil you — carry you off as plunder — through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men, after the rudiments of the world, and not after Christ. The last clause is the test, and it is not a ban on the discipline. A theology is captive when its first principles were set somewhere other than in Christ, whatever vocabulary it uses afterwards; and a church that despises philosophy usually has one anyway, absorbed from the age and never examined because it was never named.
roots_summary: Greek philosophos (G5386), a philosopher; philosophia (G5385), philosophy; spermologos (G4691), a babbler, seed-picker; sophia tou kosmou (G4678), the wisdom of this world.
roots_lines: Greek philosophos (G5386) — philosopher; Acts 17:18 only.
Greek philosophia (G5385) — philosophy; Colossians 2:8 only, paired with kenes apates, vain deceit.
Greek spermologos (G4691) — babbler, one who picks up scraps; Acts 17:18 — the Athenians' word for Paul.
usage: “Certain philosophers of the Epicureans, and of the Stoicks, encountered him” — and he stayed.
“As certain also of your own poets have said” — quoted approvingly, on Mars' hill.
“Spoil you through philosophy… and not after Christ” — the last clause is the test.

pos: n. pl. (professional teachers of rhetoric who taught men to win arguments; in Calvin, a name for the scholastic disputers)
etymology: Greek sophistes, a master of one's craft, a wise man — the honourable sense soured because the fifth-century Athenian teachers sold the art of making the weaker case appear the stronger.
biblical_def: A sophist is a man skilled at making an argument win rather than at making it true; Calvin uses the word constantly of the scholastic disputers of his day. Scripture names the type without the label: “where is the disputer of this world?” (1Co 1:20); the man who dotes “about questions and strifes of words, whereof cometh envy, strife, railings, evil surmisings” (1Ti 6:4); the charge to Timothy to avoid “profane and vain babblings, and oppositions of science falsely so called” (1Ti 6:20), and to strive not about words “to no profit, but to the subverting of the hearers” (2Ti 2:14). Paul's own refusal is the counter-model: “my speech and my preaching was not with enticing words of man's wisdom” (1Co 2:4).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines sophist as a professor of philosophy; and, in a lower sense, a captious or fallacious reasoner; and sophistry as fallacious reasoning, reasoning sound in appearance only.
webster_full: SOPHIST, n. A professor of philosophy; as the sophists of Greece.
2. A captious or fallacious reasoner.
SOPHISTRY, n. Fallacious reasoning; reasoning sound in appearance only.
scriptures: Where is the wise? where is the scribe? where is the disputer of this world? hath not God made foolish the wisdom of this world?
He is proud, knowing nothing, but doting about questions and strifes of words, whereof cometh envy, strife, railings, evil surmisings,
O Timothy, keep that which is committed to thy trust, avoiding profane and vain babblings, and oppositions of science falsely so called:
Of these things put them in remembrance, charging them before the Lord that they strive not about words to no profit, but to the subverting of the hearers.
And my speech and my preaching was not with enticing words of man's wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power:
corruption_summary: Skill in argument is taken for soundness in doctrine, and Paul deliberately declined the enticing words that would have won him a hearing.
corruption_paragraphs: First Corinthians 2:4 is a decision, not a limitation. Paul could argue — Acts is full of him reasoning, disputing and persuading — and at Corinth he chose against the technique the city admired, so that their faith “should not stand in the wisdom of men, but in the power of God” (1Co 2:5). The reasoning is pastoral: a congregation won by rhetorical skill is held by rhetorical skill, and will be taken from you by the next man who has more of it. Every ministry built on a communicator has this problem waiting in it.

The sophist's mark in 1 Timothy 6:4 is not error but appetite — doting about questions and strifes of words — and the fruit named is envy, strife, railings and evil surmisings, which are relational rather than doctrinal. That is the reliable test, because a sophist may hold every article correctly. Ask not whether the man is right but what grows around him; 2 Timothy 2:14 says the strife of words works to the subverting of the hearers, and the hearers usually feel it before they can name it.
roots_summary: Greek suzetetes (G4804), a disputer; logomachia (G3055), a strife of words; peithois logois (G3981), enticing words; kenophonia (G2757), vain babbling.
roots_lines: Greek suzetetes (G4804) — disputer; 1 Corinthians 1:20 only.
Greek logomachia (G3055) — strife of words; 1 Timothy 6:4 only; the verb logomacheo (G3054), 2 Timothy 2:14.
Greek kenophonia (G2757) — vain babbling; 1 Timothy 6:20, 2 Timothy 2:16.
usage: “Where is the disputer of this world?” — the type without the label.
“Doting about questions and strifes of words” — the mark is appetite, not error.
“Not with enticing words of man's wisdom” — a decision by a man who could have.

pos: n. pl. (those who study and teach the doctrine of God)
etymology: Greek theos, God, and logos, word or account — theology is an account of God. The older English is divines, and the Westminster Assembly called its members that.
biblical_def: A theologian is one who gives an account of God, and Scripture treats the work as an office with a standard: “Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth” (2Ti 2:15); an elder must be “holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught, that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers” (Tit 1:9); and the charge is personal before it is public: “Take heed unto thyself, and unto the doctrine; continue in them: for in doing this thou shalt both save thyself, and them that hear thee” (1Ti 4:16). The warning attached is heavier than for other trades: “be not many masters, knowing that we shall receive the greater condemnation” (Jas 3:1).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines theologian as a divine; a person well versed in theology, or a professor of divinity; and theology as divinity, or the science of God and divine things.
webster_full: THEOLOGIAN, n. A divine; a person well versed in theology, or a professor of divinity.

THEOLOGY, n. Divinity; the science of God and divine things; or the science which teaches the existence, character and attributes of God, his laws and government, the doctrines we are to believe, and the duties we are to practice.
scriptures: Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth.
Tit 1:9
Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught, that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers.
Take heed unto thyself, and unto the doctrine; continue in them: for in doing this thou shalt both save thyself, and them that hear thee.
Jas 3:1
My brethren, be not many masters, knowing that we shall receive the greater condemnation.
If any man teach otherwise, and consent not to wholesome words, even the words of our Lord Jesus Christ, and to the doctrine which is according to godliness;
corruption_summary: Theology is treated as a specialism for the academy, and every Christian has one; the only question is whether it is examined.
corruption_paragraphs: The commonest error is the assumption that theology belongs to a guild — that ordinary believers have faith while scholars have doctrine. Everyone who prays has a theology; the prayer assumes things about who God is, whether He hears, and what He may be asked. An unexamined theology is not an absent one, and it is usually assembled from hymns, half-remembered sermons and the surrounding culture. Webster's definition is the useful corrective: the science which teaches the existence, character and attributes of God, His laws and government, the doctrines we are to believe and the duties we are to practise. That is a description of what every Christian needs, not of what a few may specialise in.

The guild's own corruption is in James 3:1, and it is stated as a deterrent: be not many masters, knowing that we shall receive the greater condemnation — and James includes himself in the we. Theology done as a career, with a reputation to protect and a position to defend, is a peculiarly dangerous trade, because a man may spend a life handling the things of God with no more reverence than a clerk handles a ledger. First Timothy 4:16 puts the two duties in the order that guards against it: take heed unto thyself, and unto the doctrine — the man first.
roots_summary: Greek didaskalos (G1320), teacher, master; orthotomeo (G3718), to cut straight, rightly divide; hugiainousa didaskalia (G5198, G1319), sound doctrine.
roots_lines: Greek orthotomeo (G3718) — to rightly divide, cut straight; 2 Timothy 2:15 only.
Greek didaskalos (G1320) — teacher; James 3:1, Ephesians 4:11, 1 Timothy 2:7.
Greek hugiainousa didaskalia (G5198 with G1319) — sound doctrine; Titus 1:9, 2:1, 1 Timothy 1:10, 2 Timothy 4:3.
usage: “Rightly dividing the word of truth” — the standard of the trade.
“Take heed unto thyself, and unto the doctrine” — the man named first.
“Be not many masters” — a deterrent, with James inside it.

pos: n. (Athenian philosopher, c. 428–348 BC, whose thought shaped much of the church's later vocabulary)
etymology: Greek Platon. Calvin cites him more often and more respectfully than any other pagan, and criticises the theologians who let him govern where Scripture should.
biblical_def: Plato is not named in Scripture, but his school is: Paul met the Stoicks and Epicureans at Athens (Act 17:18) in the city Plato had taught in, and quoted their poets to them (Act 17:28). The Bible's judgment on that whole enterprise is double. It grants a real knowledge: “that which may be known of God is manifest in them; for God hath shewed it unto them” (Rom 1:19). And it denies that the knowledge saves: “after that in the wisdom of God the world by wisdom knew not God, it pleased God by the foolishness of preaching to save them that believe” (1Co 1:21).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines Platonic as pertaining to Plato or his philosophy, his school or opinions; and Platonism as the philosophy of Plato, and his doctrines.
webster_full: PLATONIC, a. Pertaining to Plato, or to his philosophy, his school or his opinions.
PLATONISM, n. The philosophy of Plato, consisting of three branches, theology, physics and mathematics.
2. The doctrines or opinions of Plato.
scriptures: Then certain philosophers of the Epicureans, and of the Stoicks, encountered him. And some said, What will this babbler say? other some, He seemeth to be a setter forth of strange gods: because he preached unto them Jesus, and the resurrection.
Rom 1:19
Because that which may be known of God is manifest in them; for God hath shewed it unto them.
For after that in the wisdom of God the world by wisdom knew not God, it pleased God by the foolishness of preaching to save them that believe.
For in him we live, and move, and have our being; as certain also of your own poets have said, For we are also his offspring.
Col 2:8
Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men, after the rudiments of the world, and not after Christ.
corruption_summary: Platonic ideas have entered the church wearing biblical clothes, and the plainest of them is a hope of escaping the body rather than of rising in it.
corruption_paragraphs: The most successful Platonism in the church is the doctrine of the afterlife that most Christians actually hold: an immortal soul escaping a body that was always a hindrance, going to a realm of pure spirit. That is Plato, and it is not the creed. The New Testament's hope is a resurrection — “this mortal must put on immortality” (1Co 15:53) — and its verdict on the body is that God made it, Christ took one, and it is to be raised and glorified. A funeral address that consoles a family entirely with the soul's release has borrowed from the Academy without meaning to.

The same current runs through the low view of matter that surfaces whenever Christians treat the physical as second-rate: work, food, marriage, art and the created world as concessions to be tolerated while the real business is inward. Genesis calls creation very good, Paul calls the prohibition of meats and marriage a doctrine of devils, and the Word became flesh. Where the church has despised the body it has always paid, most often in one of two directions — a sour asceticism, or the licence that says what is done in the body does not matter.

None of that is a reason to despise the man. Romans 1:19 concedes that what may be known of God is plain to the pagan mind, and Plato saw a great deal of it: that the world is ordered, that the good is real and not merely preferred, that the soul is not the same as the appetites. Calvin quotes him with respect and then draws the line the Bible draws — the world by wisdom knew not God. Seeing that there is a light is not the same as knowing whose it is.
roots_lines: Greek sophia tou kosmou (G4678) — the wisdom of the world; 1 Corinthians 1:20–21, 3:19.
Greek anastasis (G386) — resurrection; Acts 17:18, 17:32 — the doctrine that emptied the Areopagus.
Greek thnetos (G2349) — mortal; 1 Corinthians 15:53–54, 2 Corinthians 5:4.
usage: “The world by wisdom knew not God” — the limit of the Academy.
“That which may be known of God is manifest in them” — and it was, in part.
“When they heard of the resurrection of the dead, some mocked” — where Athens stopped.

pos: n. (Peter Lombard, c. 1096–1160, bishop of Paris, author of the Sentences, the standard theology textbook of the Middle Ages)
etymology: From Lombardy, his birthplace. Called the Master of the Sentences; every medieval theologian of note, including Aquinas, lectured on his book before writing his own.
biblical_def: Peter Lombard compiled the Four Books of Sentences — a topical arrangement of Scripture and the fathers, especially Augustine — which became the textbook every theologian commented on for four hundred years. Calvin cites him more than any other schoolman, agreeing where he follows Augustine and objecting where he does not. His book is the reason the medieval church had seven sacraments, since his enumeration became the standard. The Reformed test of any such compilation is Paul's: “other foundation can no man lay than that is laid, which is Jesus Christ” (1Co 3:11), and Berea's: “they searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so” (Act 17:11).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines sentence as a determination or decision given by a court; an opinion; a maxim; a short saying containing moral instruction; and, in grammar, a period, a number of words containing complete sense.
webster_full: SENTENCE, n. Judgment pronounced; determination or decision given by a court.
2. In language, a maxim; an axiom; a short saying containing moral instruction.
3. An opinion; a determination.
4. In grammar, a period; a number of words containing complete sense, and followed by a full stop.
scriptures: For other foundation can no man lay than that is laid, which is Jesus Christ.
These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.
All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:
Col 2:8
Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men, after the rudiments of the world, and not after Christ.
Mar 7:8
For laying aside the commandment of God, ye hold the tradition of men, as the washing of pots and cups: and many other such like things ye do.
corruption_summary: A textbook becomes the syllabus and then the authority, and four centuries of theologians commented on Lombard rather than on Scripture.
corruption_paragraphs: The Sentences did real service: it gathered the fathers, arranged the questions, and gave Europe a common frame for theological work. Its corruption was structural rather than doctrinal. Because a young theologian's first task was to lecture on Lombard, the discipline organised itself around a commentary tradition; the questions were his questions, the divisions his divisions, and originality meant a fresh answer within his scheme rather than a fresh look at the text. Whole doctrines — the sevenfold sacraments among them — entered the church's mind because they were where he had put them.

That is the standing danger of every systematic arrangement, including the Reformed ones. A confession, a systematic theology, a study Bible's notes: each is a good servant and each can quietly become the lens through which the text is read, so that a man finds in Romans what his system requires and never notices the verses it has no slot for. The Bereans are the antidote and they were applying the test to an apostle. A tradition that cannot be checked against the Scriptures has stopped being a help and has become a second authority, whatever it says about itself.
roots_summary: Greek themelios (G2310), foundation; anakrino (G350), to examine, search; paradosis (G3862), tradition; theopneustos (G2315), God-breathed.
roots_lines: Greek themelios (G2310) — foundation; 1 Corinthians 3:11, Ephesians 2:20.
Greek anakrino (G350) — to examine, search; Acts 17:11, 1 Corinthians 2:15, 4:3.
Greek paradosis (G3862) — tradition; Mark 7:8–9, Colossians 2:8; and of apostolic teaching, 2 Thessalonians 2:15.
usage: “They searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so” — applied to an apostle.
“Other foundation can no man lay” — the test of every arrangement.
“Laying aside the commandment of God, ye hold the tradition of men” — how a textbook becomes an authority.

pos: n. pl. (followers of Mani, third-century Persian teacher of a dualism of two eternal principles, light and darkness)
etymology: From Mani (c. 216–276), who taught that good and evil are two co-eternal powers and that matter is the work of the dark one. Augustine was a Manichee for nine years before his conversion, which is why he writes against them so well.
biblical_def: The Manichees held two eternal principles, so that evil is a substance and matter its product. Scripture allows no second eternal power: “I form the light, and create darkness: I make peace, and create evil: I the LORD do all these things” (Isa 45:7); “God saw every thing that he had made, and, behold, it was very good” (Gen 1:31); “every creature of God is good, and nothing to be refused, if it be received with thanksgiving” (1Ti 4:4). Evil in the Bible is not a thing made but a good thing corrupted, entering by a will: “by one man sin entered into the world” (Rom 5:12). And God is light “and in him is no darkness at all” (1Jn 1:5).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines Manichean as one of a sect in Persia, who maintained that there are two principles, the one good and the other evil, each of which is eternal.
webster_full: MANICHEAN, MANICHEE, n. One of a sect in Persia, who maintained that there are two principles, the one the cause of good, the other of evil; both eternal, and both independent.
MANICHEISM, n. The doctrines of the Manicheans.
scriptures: Isa 45:7
I form the light, and create darkness: I make peace, and create evil: I the LORD do all these things.
Gen 1:31
And God saw every thing that he had made, and, behold, it was very good. And the evening and the morning were the sixth day.
For every creature of God is good, and nothing to be refused, if it be received with thanksgiving:
Rom 5:12
Wherefore, as by one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin; and so death passed upon all men, for that all have sinned:
This then is the message which we have heard of him, and declare unto you, that God is light, and in him is no darkness at all.
corruption_summary: Evil is made a rival power with its own existence, and Scripture gives it no substance and no eternity.
corruption_paragraphs: Dualism is permanently attractive because it solves the problem of evil at a stroke: God is not responsible, because another power is. The cost is the whole doctrine of God. A deity with a co-eternal rival is not sovereign, not infinite, and cannot promise an outcome; Isaiah 45:7 was spoken to Cyrus in the heartland of Persian dualism precisely to deny it, and its claim is deliberately uncomfortable — I make peace, and create evil, I the LORD do all these things. The Reformed have never softened it to mean that God is the author of sin; they have held that He ordains what He does not approve, and that the mystery of that is preferable to a second god.

The practical Manicheism in the church is a low view of matter, and it survives long after the sect is forgotten — the assumption that the body is the problem, that the spiritual is the immaterial, that a Christian is holiest when least embodied. Every part of Scripture resists it: the creation pronounced very good, the incarnation, the resurrection of the body, the wedding at Cana, the command to receive meats with thanksgiving. Where the church has drifted toward Mani it has usually produced either asceticism or licence, and often both in the same generation, since a body that does not matter may be either starved or indulged.
roots_summary: Hebrew bara (H1254), to create; ra (H7451), evil, calamity; Greek ktisma (G2938), a creature, thing created; skotia (G4653), darkness.
roots_lines: Hebrew bara (H1254) — to create; Isaiah 45:7, Genesis 1:1, 1:27.
Hebrew ra (H7451) — evil, adversity, calamity; Isaiah 45:7, Amos 3:6, Job 2:10.
Greek ktisma (G2938) — creature, thing created; 1 Timothy 4:4, James 1:18, Revelation 5:13.
usage: “I make peace, and create evil” — spoken into the heartland of dualism.
“Every creature of God is good” — the verse against a despised creation.
“In him is no darkness at all” — no rival, and no shadow.

pos: n. (Michael Servetus, 1511–1553, Spanish physician and anti-trinitarian, burned at Geneva)
etymology: Latinised form of Miguel Serveto. He published On the Errors of the Trinity at twenty, and was condemned by Rome and by the Reformed alike before his death at Geneva.
biblical_def: Servetus denied the Trinity, holding the Son and the Spirit to be modes or manifestations rather than distinct Persons. The doctrine he denied is stated in the baptismal formula, one name and three: “baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost” (Mat 28:19); in the Word who “was with God, and… was God” (John 1:1); in the benediction that names all three (2Co 13:14); and at the Jordan, where the Son is baptised, the Spirit descends, and the Father speaks (Mat 3:16–17). His execution is the permanent stain on the Reformed record and is dealt with plainly below.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for Servetus; his definition of heresy is the relevant one: a fundamental error in religion, or an error of opinion respecting some fundamental doctrine of religion.
webster_full: HERESY, n. A fundamental error in religion, or an error of opinion respecting some fundamental doctrine of religion.
2. Heresy, in law, is an offense against Christianity, consisting in a denial of some of its essential doctrines, publicly avowed and obstinately maintained.
scriptures: Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost:
John 1:1
In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.
The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the communion of the Holy Ghost, be with you all. Amen.
Mat 3:16
And Jesus, when he was baptized, went up straightway out of the water: and, lo, the heavens were opened unto him, and he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove, and lighting upon him:
Luk 9:55
But he turned, and rebuked them, and said, Ye know not what manner of spirit ye are of.
corruption_summary: The case is used to dismiss Calvin entirely or is defended as a necessity of the age, and neither answer is honest.
corruption_paragraphs: Two dishonest treatments of Servetus circulate, and this dictionary should hold neither. The first uses the burning to void everything Calvin wrote, as though a man's exegesis of Romans were refuted by his conduct in 1553. The second defends the execution as the ordinary practice of the age — true as history, since Rome had already condemned him and would have done the same, and the city council rather than Calvin passed the sentence — and then treats that context as a justification. It is an explanation and not a justification, and the distinction matters.

The plain judgment is that it was wrong: wrong because the civil sword has no jurisdiction over heresy, which is the very principle the Reformed later came to hold and which the Second London Confession states in its chapter on liberty of conscience; and wrong because the Lord had already answered the question when two disciples proposed fire for a village that refused Him, and He turned and rebuked them, saying, ye know not what manner of spirit ye are of (Luk 9:55). Servetus's doctrine was fatal error and the church was right to refuse it. The fire was not the church's to light.

The doctrine itself is worth stating, because anti-trinitarianism keeps returning under new names. Servetus's objection was that Trinity is unbiblical language, which is true of the word and false of the content: one God, and the Father sends, the Son is sent, and the Spirit proceeds; each is called God, and they are distinguished in the same sentences that unite them. The vocabulary was framed precisely because men kept finding ways to say God while meaning something less, and the creeds are the church's record of every such attempt and its answer.
roots_summary: Greek onoma (G3686), name — singular in Matthew 28:19 with three genitives; hupostasis (G5287), person, substance; hairesis (G139), heresy, a chosen party.
roots_lines: Greek eis to onoma (G3686) — into the name; Matthew 28:19 — one name, three Persons.
Greek hupostasis (G5287) — person; Hebrews 1:3, the express image of his person.
Greek hairesis (G139) — heresy, sect; Galatians 5:20, 2 Peter 2:1, Titus 3:10.
usage: “In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost” — one name, three.
“Ye know not what manner of spirit ye are of” — said to disciples who proposed fire.
“A man that is an heretick… reject” — the apostolic penalty, and it is not the stake.

pos: n. (Andreas Osiander, 1498–1552, Lutheran reformer who taught that justification is by the indwelling essential righteousness of Christ)
etymology: German reformer of Nuremberg, later of Königsberg. Calvin devotes a long section of the Institutes to refuting him, and the dispute clarified what the Reformation meant by an imputed righteousness.
biblical_def: Osiander held that a man is justified because Christ's divine nature dwells in him and communicates its own essential righteousness — a righteousness infused rather than reckoned. The Reformed answer is that justification is a verdict, not an infusion: “to him that worketh not, but believeth on him that justifieth the ungodly, his faith is counted for righteousness” (Rom 4:5); “he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him” (2Co 5:21); the believer is “found in him, not having mine own righteousness, which is of the law, but that which is through the faith of Christ, the righteousness which is of God by faith” (Php 3:9). The indwelling is real and is sanctification, which follows.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines impute as to charge, to attribute, to set to the account of; and, in theology, to attribute or set to the account of one what does not properly belong to him, as the righteousness of Christ to believers.
webster_full: IMPUTE, v.t. To charge; to attribute; to set to the account of.
2. To attribute; to ascribe.
3. In theology, to impute is to charge, attribute or set to the account of; as, to impute the sin of Adam to his posterity, or the righteousness of Christ to believers.
scriptures: Rom 4:5
But to him that worketh not, but believeth on him that justifieth the ungodly, his faith is counted for righteousness.
For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him.
Php 3:9
And be found in him, not having mine own righteousness, which is of the law, but that which is through the faith of Christ, the righteousness which is of God by faith:
Rom 4:6
Even as David also describeth the blessedness of the man, unto whom God imputeth righteousness without works,
Gal 2:20

I am crucified with Christ: nevertheless I live; yet not I, but Christ liveth in me: and the life which I now live in the flesh I live by the faith of the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself for me.
corruption_summary: Justification and sanctification are run together, and Osiander's error is the one modern preaching most often repeats by accident.
corruption_paragraphs: Osiander was not a liberal; he was a reformer who wanted a righteousness more real than a bare reckoning, and thought imputation sounded like a legal fiction. Calvin's reply is that the reckoning is the most real thing about a believer's standing, because God's verdict constitutes reality rather than merely describing it; and that a righteousness which is in the man will be, in this life, a partial and growing thing, so that a justification resting on it can never be complete. Philippians 3:9 puts the believer's righteousness outside him twice over: not mine own, but that which is of God, and he is found in Him when he has it.

The error is worth naming because most congregations hear a version of it without any Lutheran history attached — preaching in which the believer's acceptance rises and falls with his transformation, so that a bad fortnight puts his standing in doubt. That is Osiander in practice, and its pastoral fruit is either despair or self-deception. The Reformed order is fixed and it is a mercy: justified by a righteousness not his own, therefore free to be sanctified by a Christ who genuinely indwells him. Galatians 2:20 has both — Christ liveth in me, and the life I now live I live by the faith of the Son of God — and never confuses which one does the justifying.
roots_summary: Greek logizomai (G3049), to reckon, count, impute; dikaioo (G1344), to justify, declare righteous; dikaiosune (G1343), righteousness.
roots_lines: Greek logizomai (G3049) — to count, impute; Romans 4:3, 4:5–6, 4:8, 4:22–24.
Greek dikaioo (G1344) — to justify, declare righteous; Romans 3:24, 4:5, 5:1, 8:30.
Greek dikaiosune ek theou (G1343) — the righteousness which is of God; Philippians 3:9, Romans 1:17.
usage: “His faith is counted for righteousness” — a reckoning, and it constitutes reality.
“Not having mine own righteousness” — outside the man, twice over.
“Christ liveth in me” — real indwelling, and it is not what justifies.

pos: n. and v. (a frivolous objection raised to evade rather than to understand)
etymology: Latin cavillari, to jeer, to quibble. A cavil is not an honest difficulty; it is an objection whose purpose is to avoid the conclusion.
biblical_def: A cavil is an objection raised to escape rather than to learn, and the Gospels are full of them. “Master, which is the great commandment in the law?” is asked by a lawyer “tempting him” (Mat 22:35–36); the Sadducees, “which say that there is no resurrection”, bring a woman with seven husbands (Mat 22:23–28); the lawyer of Luke 10, “willing to justify himself”, asks, And who is my neighbour? (Luk 10:29). Paul's instruction to Timothy is to decline the game: “foolish and unlearned questions avoid, knowing that they do gender strifes” (2Ti 2:23), and to Titus, “avoid foolish questions… for they are unprofitable and vain” (Tit 3:9).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines cavil as to raise captious and frivolous objections; and, as a noun, a false or frivolous objection.
webster_full: CAVIL, v.i. To raise captious and frivolous objections; to find fault without good reason.
CAVIL, n. False or frivolous objections; also, a mere quibble.
CAVILER, n. One who cavils; one who is apt to raise captious objections; a captious disputant.
scriptures: Then one of them, which was a lawyer, asked him a question, tempting him, and saying,
But he, willing to justify himself, said unto Jesus, And who is my neighbour?
But foolish and unlearned questions avoid, knowing that they do gender strifes.
Tit 3:9
But avoid foolish questions, and genealogies, and contentions, and strivings about the law; for they are unprofitable and vain.
The same day came to him the Sadducees, which say that there is no resurrection, and asked him,
corruption_summary: An honest doubt is treated as a cavil and a cavil as an honest doubt, and the Lord answered the first and refused the second.
corruption_paragraphs: The Lord's practice is the model and it distinguishes sharply. To the honest — Nicodemus by night, the man who said Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief, Thomas who wanted to see the hands — He gives more than was asked. To the caviller He often gives nothing, or a counter-question, or silence: He would not tell the chief priests by what authority He acted, because they would not answer His question about John's baptism first. Discernment between the two is a pastoral necessity, and getting it wrong in either direction does real damage — crushing a doubter as though he were a scoffer, or spending years arguing with a man who has no intention of being persuaded.

The tell is usually motive rather than content, and Luke 10:29 names it in five words: willing to justify himself. The lawyer's question — and who is my neighbour? — is a good question, one a seminary would set an essay on, and it was asked to narrow the obligation rather than to meet it. The Lord answers with a story that makes the question unanswerable in the form it was asked, and sends him away with a command instead. That is how a cavil is best handled: not by conceding it and not by refusing to speak, but by returning something the caviller cannot file away.
roots_summary: Greek peirazo (G3985), to tempt, test with intent; zetesis (G2214), a questioning; moros (G3474), foolish; apaideutos (G521), unlearned, undisciplined.
roots_lines: Greek peirazo (G3985) — tempting; Matthew 22:35, 16:1, 19:3, Mark 10:2.
Greek zetesis (G2214) — questioning, dispute; 2 Timothy 2:23, 1 Timothy 6:4, Titus 3:9.
Greek apaideutos (G521) — unlearned, uninstructed; 2 Timothy 2:23 only.
usage: “Willing to justify himself” — the motive behind a good question.
“Foolish and unlearned questions avoid” — permission to decline the game.
“Neither tell I you by what authority” — the Lord's answer to men who would not answer.

pos: n. (false accusation maliciously made; slander uttered to destroy a reputation)
etymology: Latin calumnia, a false accusation, from calvi, to deceive. The Roman law punished the accuser who brought a charge he knew to be false, and branded him on the forehead.
biblical_def: Calumny is false accusation with malice in it. The Law forbids it three ways: “Thou shalt not raise a false report” (Exo 23:1); “Thou shalt not go up and down as a talebearer among thy people” (Lev 19:16); and the ninth commandment, “Thou shalt not bear false witness against thy neighbour” (Exo 20:16). David knew it: “I have heard the slander of many: fear was on every side” (Psa 31:13). The Lord makes it a beatitude when it is suffered for His sake: “Blessed are ye, when men shall revile you, and persecute you, and shall say all manner of evil against you falsely, for my sake” (Mat 5:11). And the accuser of the brethren is named (Rev 12:10).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines calumny as slander; false accusation of a crime or offense, knowingly or maliciously made or reported, to the injury of another.
webster_full: CALUMNY, n. Slander; false accusation of a crime or offense, knowingly or maliciously made or reported, to the injury of another; false representation of facts reproachful to another, made by design, and with knowledge of its falsehood.
scriptures: Exo 23:1
Thou shalt not raise a false report: put not thine hand with the wicked to be an unrighteous witness.
Thou shalt not go up and down as a talebearer among thy people: neither shalt thou stand against the blood of thy neighbour: I am the LORD.
Thou shalt not bear false witness against thy neighbour.
For I have heard the slander of many: fear was on every side: while they took counsel together against me, they devised to take away my life.
Mat 5:11
Blessed are ye, when men shall revile you, and persecute you, and shall say all manner of evil against you falsely, for my sake.
corruption_summary: Calumny is passed along by people who would never invent it, and Exodus forbids the raising of a false report and the hearing of it in one verse.
corruption_paragraphs: Exodus 23:1 has a second clause that indicts most of the church: thou shalt not raise a false report; put not thine hand with the wicked to be an unrighteous witness. The sin is not confined to the inventor. The man who repeats what he has not verified, who forwards the message, who says only that he is concerned and asks for prayer while naming the charge, has put his hand with the wicked and supplied the thing every calumny requires, which is circulation. Leviticus 19:16 uses a walking word — go up and down as a talebearer — because the tale needs feet.

Scripture's protection for the accused is procedural and the church routinely ignores it. An accusation against an elder is not to be received but before two or three witnesses (1Ti 5:19); a matter is established at the mouth of two or three (Deu 19:15); and the false witness in Deuteronomy 19:19 receives the penalty he sought for his brother. A congregation that acts on an anonymous letter, or that treats an accusation as evidence because the charge is grave, has abandoned a standard God gave for exactly the cases where feeling runs highest.

The comfort in Matthew 5:11 is precise and it is not a licence. Blessed are ye when men shall say all manner of evil against you falsely, for my sake — two conditions. A man suffering criticism he has earned is not being persecuted, and a man disliked for his temper rather than his Master is not in the beatitude. Where both conditions hold, the instruction is to rejoice, and Peter's addition is the pattern: when He suffered, He threatened not, but committed Himself to Him that judgeth righteously.
roots_summary: Hebrew dibbah (H1681), an evil report, slander; rakil (H7400), a talebearer; ed shaqer (H5707, H8267), a false witness; Greek diabolos (G1228), accuser, slanderer.
roots_lines: Hebrew dibbah (H1681) — evil report, slander; Psalm 31:13, Numbers 13:32, Proverbs 10:18.
Hebrew rakil (H7400) — talebearer; Leviticus 19:16, Proverbs 11:13, 18:8, 20:19.
Greek diabolos (G1228) — slanderer, accuser; 1 Timothy 3:11, 2 Timothy 3:3, Titus 2:3; and of Satan, Revelation 12:10.
usage: “Put not thine hand with the wicked” — the clause that indicts the repeater.
“Go up and down as a talebearer” — the tale needs feet.
“Say all manner of evil against you falsely, for my sake” — two conditions on the beatitude.
